analysis.one_liner: Expands federal aid that caps deductibles and copays for people buying Marketplace health plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 20, 2026 by Rep. Kim Schrier with one cosponsor, the bill has been referred to two House committees and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill makes the ACA's cost-sharing reductions much more generous. Starting in 2028, subsidized Marketplace plans must cover a larger share of medical bills, roughly gold-level coverage instead of silver-level, and eligibility for that richer cost-sharing would stretch up to 400% of the poverty line instead of stopping at 250%. It also bases premium tax credits on the second-lowest-cost gold plan rather than silver, making credits larger, and it writes a blank-check appropriation to pay insurers for the richer benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with incomes between roughly 150% and 400% of the poverty line who buy their own coverage on the ACA Marketplaces. Today many of them face plans that leave thousands of dollars in deductibles and copays; the bill would require insurers to pick up 85–87% of allowed medical costs for this group, with the federal government reimbursing the difference. Health insurers would also gain, since they are paid by the federal government to deliver the richer coverage.

how_it_helps.text: From plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, cost-sharing reductions must be applied as if the benchmark were gold-level coverage rather than silver-level, meaning enrollees' plans would cover a larger share of their medical bills.

The bill raises insurers' required share of allowed costs to 87% for households up to 300% of the poverty line and 85% for households up to 400% of the poverty line, extending richer cost-sharing well beyond the current 250% cutoff, where it now tapers to 70–73%.

Premium tax credits would be calculated against the second-lowest-cost gold plan instead of silver, increasing the credit amounts available to subsidized enrollees, effective for taxable years after December 31, 2027.
The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' from the Treasury to pay for the expanded cost-sharing reductions, with no spending cap.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill funds the expanded subsidies with open-ended appropriations and includes no revenue offsets, so the cost would add to federal deficits in whatever amount the expanded coverage requires.

drawbacks.text: The funding section appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar limit and no offsetting revenue, so the bill's total cost is uncapped and would add to federal deficits.

Requiring plans to cover 85–87% of medical costs raises claims costs for insurers; unless payments fully keep pace, richer required coverage can push up premiums, and basing tax credits on gold plans rather than silver can raise the sticker price of silver plans relative to the credit.

The bill rewrites the benchmark for state Basic Health Programs from the second-lowest-cost silver plan to gold, which changes the financing formula states rely on and could complicate those programs' budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the several million Marketplace enrollees in the 150–400% of poverty range, high deductibles are one of the biggest reasons coverage goes unused, and pushing plans toward gold-level cost-sharing addresses that directly. The serious weakness is fiscal design: an uncapped appropriation with no offsets, and an uncertainty about whether insurer payments will fully cover the higher claims burden without premium spillover. The consumer benefit is real; the financing is a blank check.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 20, 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and neither has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) introduced the bill for herself and Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D-IL) on January 20, 2026.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, the Committee on Ways and Means; the action history shows no markup, vote, or further movement after referral.
The bill has exactly one cosponsor, Rep. Budzinski, per the cosponsor list.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: because the bill has idled in two committees without a markup or vote, Marketplace enrollees keep the current lower cost-sharing levels and insurers keep collecting under the current payment structure. Nothing has changed yet either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Democrats, so how the chambers would split is unknown.

industries.note: The expanded cost-sharing reductions and the higher gold-plan premium credit benchmark flow through private Marketplace insurers, who would be federally reimbursed to deliver richer benefits. Their role as the channel for subsidized coverage would be locked in further, while enrollees get lower deductibles and copays.
Patients facing smaller deductibles and copays are more likely to get care and pay their bills, reducing uncompensated care. Providers benefit alongside enrollees.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no cosponsor momentum, and no committee action in two committees, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote unless party leadership elevates it; most health bills at this stage die quietly at the end of the Congress.
